HOSPITAL COURSE:
1. Cardiovascular:  Pump:  Patient with Class IV CHF admitted
with acute CHF exacerbation.  At initial presentation in the
ED, patient in acute respiratory distress, received Lasix
with good diuresis, and subsequent improved respiratory
status.

He initially went to the floor, where he was weaned down to 4
liters nasal cannula of oxygen.  However, the day following
admission, patient developed worsening respiratory distress
and was markedly tachypneic with decreased urine output and
abdominal pain.  He was then transferred to the MICU for
closer monitoring.

Upon arrival in the MICU, there was concern that patient
might be intervascularly dry given his hypernatremia, acute
renal failure, and free water deficit, and low CVPs.  He
received several free water and normal saline boluses.
Although his chest x-ray did show bilateral pleural
effusions, these were thought to be chronic.

However, on [**10-4**], the patient continued to have
significant respiratory distress and difficulty weaning off
the ventilator.  A CAT scan was obtained, which showed
bilateral layering effusions, pulmonary edema, and patient
was thought to be in CHF.  At this point, he was then
diuresed with Zaroxolyn and Bumex for several days without
response.  Cardiology was then consulted for evaluation of
his CHF at which point he was started on a Natrecor drip.
Initially, Bumex and Zaroxolyn were D/C'd.  Patient had
minimal diuresis.

Review of the record showed patient has had multiple episodes
of CHF refractory to diuresis.  Bumex and Zaroxolyn were
added back.  In addition, patient was started on a Lasix
drip.  He did have an adequate diuretic response on this
regimen.  He also required the addition of dobutamine given
his poor cardiac function.  A Swan was placed to monitor
patient's hemodynamics throughout this.  Multiple attempts
were made to wean him off of his drips, which were
unsuccessful.  After several days, his Lasix drip was
stopped, and he was maintained on Natrecor and dobutamine.

However, patient had significant ectopy with dobutamine, so
this was slowly weaned down.  The CHF service was also
consulted, but no further progress was able to be made in the
management of patient's CHF.

Rhythm:  Patient with biventricular pacer and defibrillator.
He was V paced throughout the hospitalization.  He was seen
by EP and his pacer rate was increased to 95 in order to
optimize his cardiac function given his severe CHF.  He had
marked ectopy on dobutamine drip, which had been added as per
his CHF.

Coronary:  Patient had no active ischemia during the
hospitalization.

2. ID:  Patient admitted having just completed treatment for
a pneumonia.  He was started on Levaquin and Cipro on
admission to cover for community acquired and aspiration
pneumonia.  When he was transferred to the MICU, his
antibiotic coverage was brought in to ceftaz, Flagyl, and
Vancomycin to cover for pneumonia.  He was treated for seven
days.

Given his continued respiratory issues, patient was bronched
with BAL cultures obtained.  These grew out only sparse MRSA
which was thought to be colonization.  Patient remained off
antibiotics for many days.  He then subsequently developed a
Pseudomonas UTI for which he was started on cefepime.

3. Pulmonary:  Patient admitted with mild respiratory
distress thought to be CHF exacerbation and pneumonia.
Following diuresis, his respiratory status initially
improved, but then upon day of transfer to the MICU, he was
markedly tachypneic with abdominal pain and decreased urine
output.  In this setting, he was electively intubated to
allow for better workup of his other issues.

Following this, multiple attempts to wean him off the
ventilator were unsuccessful.  He was then started on an
aggressive diuresis regimen.  He was finally extubated on
[**10-10**].  He had been intubated for a total of 12
days.  He did well for several days following extubation, but
in the setting of his worsening CHF, developed progressive
respiratory distress.

Following lengthy discussions with the patient and the
family, decided that patient would not be reintubated.  He
was briefly placed on BiPAP, which he did not tolerate well
and which had minimal effect on his respiratory distress.

4. Heme:  Several days into admission, the patient developed
left lower upper edema.  An ultrasound showed a new left
subclavian vein thrombus in addition to an old right IJ clot.
Patient was then started on Heparin.  Given patient's history
of GAVE syndrome, GI was consulted prior to initiation of
Heparin.  There was also concern given a recent EGD, which
showed gastritis and a few AVMs.

Following lengthy discussion with the GI team, it was decided
that the patient would benefit from Heparin.  Serial
hematocrits were followed on this regimen.  Patient with
baseline anemia due to chronic renal insufficiency, he was
maintained on Epogen and iron per his outpatient regimen.

5. Renal:  Patient with chronic renal insufficiency and
baseline creatinine of approximately 2.2.  His creatinine
remained essentially stable.  His medications were renally
dosed.  Patient did have symptoms with urinary obstruction.
The day following admission, he developed acute abdominal
pain.  A CAT scan of the abdomen showed a distended bladder.

Following catheterization, his abdominal pain resolved.
Patient had multiple issues with Foley catheter placement
thought to be due to his prostatectomy and unusual anatomy.
Multiple episodes of Foley catheter clogging and with large
bladder residuals measuring 100 cc.  Urology was consulted,
and several catheters were placed including finally a
catheter placed under cystoscopy.  Patient then had multiple
blood clots and hematuria thought to be due to Foley catheter
trauma in the setting of Heparin.

He was briefly placed on continuous bowel irrigation and his

sinus rhythm with rare PVCs.  The patient's systolic blood

Service:  CCU

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  This is an 81 year old woman who

pain at rest which was greater than before, and she said she
was experiencing some dyspnea on exertion.  She was recently
transfused two units of packed red blood cells on Friday.
Her primary care physician did routine blood work on Thursday
prior to admission with a hematocrit of 22.  Emergency
medical services took the patient the morning of admission
with substernal chest pain to [**Hospital3 **],
electrocardiogram with ST elevations and she was transferred
to [**Hospital6 256**] for catheterization.

disease, left circumflex was totally occluded in the mid
segment but with collaterals to the right coronary artery.
Right coronary artery with severe mid disease, occluded in
the more distal segment.  Percutaneous transluminal coronary
angioplasty stent of the tortuous mid left circumflex/obtuse
marginal 1.  Right heart catheterization showed a mean RA of
7, PA systolic of 46, mean wedge pressure of 28, cardiac
output of 5.14.  Transferred to the CCU for further
monitoring.  Overall better post catheterization.  With the
exception of generalized weakness and chronic cough since
[**Month (only) 1096**].

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:  Notes a 10 pound weight loss over the
last few months and dyspnea on exertion, weakness and
fatigue.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
1.  Angina.
2.  Slight stroke, resulting in temporary left Bell's palsy.
3.  Glaucoma.
4.  Hypertension.
5.  Hypercholesterolemia.

colonoscopy except for benign polyps, negative small bowel
follow-through, negative barium enema, negative small bowel
biopsy for sprue, per primary care physician.

SOCIAL HISTORY:  She lives alone.  Negative tobacco history
and occasional alcohol.  No other drugs.

blood pressure 107/43, pulse 95, respiratory rate 22,
saturations 99% on room air.  Weight 81.6 kg.  In general a
pleasant elderly woman in no acute distress.  Head, eyes,
ears, nose and throat:  Moist mucous membranes, clear
oropharynx.  Pupils equal, round and reactive to light.  Neck
was supple.  Jugulovenous distension at 10 cm.  No carotid
bruit.  Cardiovascular regular rate and rhythm.  Normal S1
and S2, II/VI apical systolic murmur.  Lungs clear to
auscultation anteriorly.  Abdomen, soft, nontender, positive
bowel sounds.  Extremities, 1+ lower extremity edema, right
groin site dressing was clean, dry and intact.  Skin with no
rashes or lesions.

LABORATORY DATA:  Laboratory data on admission revealed white
count 16.7 with 82% neutrophils, 2% bands, 7% lymphocytes.
Hematocrit 34.8, platelets 421.  Sodium 139, potassium 2.9,
chloride 103, bicarbonate 26, BUN 19, creatinine 1, glucose
217.  INR 1.3, albumin 4.5, creatinine kinase 68, troponin
0.02.  Electrocardiogram with normal sinus rhythm, normal
intervals, normal axis, [**Street Address(2) 1766**] elevations in 1, 2, V5, V6,
ST depressions in V2 and V3.  QRS of 130.  Catheterization as
above.

HOSPITAL COURSE:  This is an 81 year old woman with
hypertension, hyperlipidemia who presented with ST elevation
myocardial infarction.  She came from catheterization with
chronically occluded right coronary artery and obtuse
marginal 1 status post percutaneous transluminal coronary
angioplasty stenting of the occluded obtuse marginal 1.
Hemodynamics on catheterization showed increased wedge
pressure.

1.  ST elevation myocardial infarction - The patient with an
inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction with CK peaked in
the 1200 the morning after cardiac catheterization.
Otherwise the patient will remain stable and was started on
Aspirin and Plavix and was also started on a low dose beta
blocker which was eventually changed to Toprol XL regimen.
Initially the patient had nonsustained ventricular
tachycardia on telemetry but this resolved within 24 hours
after catheterization and repletion of her potassium.
Otherwise the patient had an echocardiogram done for follow
up which showed 30 to 35% ejection fraction, posterior
lateral akinesis and 1 to 2+ mitral regurgitation.  The
patient was started on ACE inhibitor for afterload reduction
and this was titrated up to a once a day Zestril regimen and
again the patient was titrated up on a beta blocker and
eventually switched to Toprol XL regimen.  The patient had
lipid panel sent and liver function tests sent which were
normal and the patient was started on 80 q. day of
Atorvastatin.

2.  Chronic cough - The patient was noted to have a chronic
cough in the past since [**Month (only) 1096**].  The patient was otherwise
stable except for asymptomatic.  The patient had a chest
x-ray which was normal.  The patient had a follow up
computerized tomography scan which results are still pending
at the time of this discharge summary, but this can be
followed up.  The patient had one episode of blood-tinged
sputum which was likely described as a coughing exacerbation.
Secondary to increase in cough started on Guaifenesin for
symptomatic relief.

3.  Anemia - The patient with known anemia and chronic guaiac
positive stools, gastrointestinal workup as an outpatient.
Next step will be endoscopy which she can have with an
outpatient gastroenterologist.  The patient was transfused a
total of 2 units of packed red blood cells during her stay.
The patient also had one atypical blast cell on her complete
blood count the morning after cardiac catheterization and
myocardial infarction.  The patient had follow up
differentials which did not show any further atypical cells.
The patient was seen by the Hematology Service and this can
be continued to be followed as an outpatient, but as she had
no further episodes, was attributed to acute inflammatory
state after her myocardial infarction.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
1.  Inferior myocardial infarction.
2.  Decreased ejection fraction.
3.  Increased fluid overload.
4.  Anemia.
5.  Chronic cough.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
1.  Aspirin 325 p.o. q. day.
2.  Plavix 75 p.o. q. day.
3.  Atorvastatin 80 p.o. q. day.
4.  Lansoprazole.
5.  Toprol XL 25 p.o. q. day.
6.  Lasix 80 mg p.o. q. day.
7.  Spironolactone 25 mg p.o. q. day.
8.  Lisinopril 10 mg p.o. q. day.
9.  Guaifenesin 5 to 10 ml p.o. q. 4-6 hours prn.

FOLLOW UP:  The patient is to follow up with her primary care
physician in seven to ten days.  The patient is to follow up
with her cardiologist in one to two weeks.  The patient is to
continue with physical therapy as directed.

1. Hypothermia: Patient presented from group home with
temperature found to be 93F rectal on initial presentation.
Potential considered etiologies of patient's hypothermia
included hypothyroidism, hypoadrenalism, hypopituitarism,
hypothalamic dysfunction related to seizure, drug-induced, or
inactivity. Her degree of hypothermia was mild without
electrolyte or EKG abnormalities. Lipase was normal, pointing
away from pancreatitis. Infectious cause was considered but WBC
count was normal and patient was normotensive with normal
lactate making sepsis less likely an etiology. Patient's glucose
was normal on admission (108), which ruled out hypoglycemia.
Anxiolytics could cause hypothermia, but less likely as patient
has been on ativan for a long time without frequent episodes of
hypothermia. Patient was treated with bair hugger with
improvement in her temperature, and eventually weaned off bair
hugger with maintained temperature. Endocrine work up was done
and showed normal TSH and free T4. Cortisol was also within
normal limits (PM random draw) but patient was started on
overnight stress dose hydrocortisone for empiric coverage of
hypoadrenalism with taper following thereafter. Endocrinology
felt that her steroids could be tapered down from the stress
dosing given no obvious infectious source and rapid resolution
of her hypothermia with active rewarming. Exact nature of
hypothermia may be multifactorial and has resolved without
obvious precipitating factors. She will be followed by PCP and
neurology.

2. Seizure Disorder: Patient has a long history of rather
refractory seizure disorder leading to multiple AED's and [**Age over 90 15741**]
implantation. She reportedly has multiple small seizure episodes
weekly requring activation of the [**Age over 90 15741**]. Patient possibly has
hypothermia related to hypothalamic involvement with a seizure.
Patient was continued on home antiepileptic therapies including
[**Age over 90 15741**], lamotrigine, levitiracetam, high dose progesterone, and
Zonergan. Patient had a witnessed, short lasting seizure in ED,
and another one in the ICU. We titrated Keppra to 1000 PO BID
given a witnessed grand mal seizure on [**2112-3-21**]. An infectious
source was considered as a precipitant, but no source was
identified by discharge and she had no elevated white count or
other sign or symptom of infection. She was discharged on the
increased keppra dose and neurology follow-up.

1. Secondary Hypothyroidism: Patient has long-standing
hypothyroidism and this presentation with hypothermia was
unlikely an exacerbation of that underlying condition. TSH and
free T4 were checked and were within normal limits. Her
synthroid was continued.

hydrocortisone at home, but it was initially unclear if her

   Cont to monitor MS and d/c home when appropriate, f/u with [**Hospital1 9408**] r/t any

   dysfunction. SBP never dropped below 100, MAP ranged 55-78, with HR

   output.

   ampicillin and cefepime for +U/A. CXR revealed bilat effusions R>L c/w
   CHF. Abd/pelvis CT w/o contrast preliminarily showed intraperitoneal
   free fluid and colonic wall thickening predominantly on the right c/w
   third-spacing or infectious colitis. She was transferred to the ICU for
   observation and further management of CHF and ARF.

   Access:  pt pulled L IJ. IJ bleeding on throughout shift, drsng changed

   Pt private aid will come sit with pt in am.
